subtopics.title: C Tokens, Identifiers & Data Types
subtopics.subtitle: Program structure, token kinds, identifiers, storage classes and fundamental types

concepts.text: Structure of a C Program

A C program is a collection of functions, and execution always starts at main(). Lines beginning with # are preprocessor directives handled before compilation: #include pulls in a header file that declares library functions (stdio.h for printf/scanf, string.h, math.h, stdlib.h; conio.h is a non-standard Turbo C header), and #define creates symbolic constants. In C99 main returns int, and return 0 tells the operating system the program succeeded. Every statement ends with a semicolon, and braces { } group statements into a block.
C Tokens

A token is the smallest individual unit that the compiler recognises; the compiler breaks every line into tokens before it can understand it. C has six kinds of tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and special symbols (punctuators). Whitespace and comments separate tokens but are not tokens themselves.

Names of variables, functions, arrays, labels

concepts.text: Identifier rules (asked in almost every MCQ set on tokens):
items: Must start with a letter (A-Z, a-z) or an underscore; it cannot start with a digit, so 1variable is invalid but variable1 is fine.
May contain only letters, digits and underscores: no spaces, hyphens, $, @ or other symbols (first-name and total$ are invalid).
Case-sensitive: sum, Sum and SUM are three different identifiers.
Cannot be a keyword: int is illegal as a name, but Int and INT are legal (though poor style).
C89 guarantees only the first 31 characters of an internal name are significant (63 in C99); names starting with an underscore are reserved for the compiler and library, so avoid them.

concepts.text: The 32 keywords of ANSI C (C99 added inline, restrict, _Bool, _Complex and _Imaginary):
items: auto  break  case  char  const  continue  default  do
double  else  enum  extern  float  for  goto  if
int  long  register  return  short  signed  sizeof  static
struct  switch  typedef  union  unsigned  void  volatile  while

concepts.text: Constants, literals and escape sequences:
items: Integer literals: decimal 42, octal 052 (leading 0), hexadecimal 0x2A; suffix U, L, UL or LL selects unsigned/long types (42L).
Floating literals are double by default (3.14); 3.14f is a float; scientific form 2.5e3 means 2500.0.
Character constants such as 'A' have type int in C (value 65), so sizeof('A') is 4 in C but 1 in C++.
Escape sequences inside quotes: \n newline, \t tab, \\ backslash, \' and \" quotes, \0 null, \a bell, \b backspace, \r carriage return, \xhh hex code, \ooo octal code.
const int MAX = 100; is a typed read-only variable checked by the compiler; #define MAX 100 is a textual replacement done by the preprocessor with no type and no semicolon.
enum colour {RED, GREEN, BLUE}; creates named integer constants starting at 0 unless a value is assigned; later names continue from the previous value.

concepts.text: Variables, Scope and Storage Classes

A variable is a named memory location whose declaration fixes its type and name and may give it an initial value (int count = 10;). A variable declared inside a block is local to that block; one declared outside all functions is global and visible from that point to the end of the file. Local variables without an initialiser hold garbage, while globals and statics are automatically set to zero. The storage class of a variable decides where it is stored, its default value, its scope and its lifetime.

rows: Created on block entry, destroyed on exit; the default for locals
Same as auto; faster access; the & operator cannot be applied
Whole program run; a static local keeps its value between calls; a static global is hidden from other files

concepts.text: Fundamental Data Types

rows: -128 to 127 (unsigned char: 0 to 255); stores an ASCII code

concepts.text: Type modifiers and sizing rules:
items: signed and unsigned change the range, not the size; short and long change the size. short int, long int and unsigned int may be written short, long and unsigned.
The standard only guarantees sizeof(char) = 1 and sizeof(char) <= sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long); the sizes above are the usual ones on 32-bit and 64-bit gcc/MSVC.
sizeof is a compile-time operator (not a function) that yields size_t; sizeof(int) = 4, sizeof(3.0) = 8, sizeof(3.0f) = 4, sizeof(long double) is compiler dependent (8, 12 or 16).
void means 'no value': a function that returns nothing, an empty parameter list, or a generic pointer void * that can hold any address.
Mixing types promotes the smaller operand (int + float gives float); a cast forces a conversion, so (int)3.9 is 3 (truncation, not rounding). Details are in Operators & Precedence.
C89 has no bool type; any non-zero value is true and 0 is false. C99 adds _Bool via stdbool.h (bool, true, false); C++ has a built-in 1-byte bool.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Tokens, Types and Storage

The ranges in the size table follow from counting bit patterns. An n-bit type has 2^n patterns, and an unsigned type uses all of them for 0 to 2^n - 1. A signed type in two's complement gives the top bit a weight of -2^(n-1), so it covers -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. The range is lopsided by one because zero uses up one of the non-negative patterns.

concepts.plainText: An n-bit unsigned type stores x mod 2^n; e.g. (unsigned char)300 = 300 - 256 = 44

concepts.text: Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap round: 0u - 1 is UINT_MAX, and an unsigned char holding 255 becomes 0 when 1 is added and the result is stored back. Signed overflow such as INT_MAX + 1 is undefined behaviour, and storing an out-of-range value in a signed type (200 in a signed char) is implementation-defined. Wrap-around questions are only answerable for unsigned types.

concepts.text: Type qualifiers and typedef in practice:
items: const int *p (also written int const *p): the int is read-only through p, but p itself can be pointed elsewhere.
int *const p: p is fixed to one address, but the int it points to may change; const int *const p fixes both.
volatile tells the compiler the value can change behind its back (hardware registers, signal handlers), so every read and write must really happen; const volatile suits a read-only hardware port.
typedef is a compiler-level alias: after typedef char *STR; the declaration STR a, b; makes two pointers, whereas #define PSTR char * turns PSTR a, b; into char *a, b; and b is a plain char.
In C a const int variable is not a constant expression, so it cannot be a case label; an enumeration constant or a #define macro can. C++ relaxes this rule.

concepts.text: Common mistakes and special cases:
items: 08 and 09 are compile errors: a leading 0 means octal, and octal digits stop at 7.
An octal escape takes at most three digits, so \1234 is \123 followed by 4; a hex escape keeps reading hex digits, so \x41B is one value (0x41B) that does not fit in a char.
Whether plain char is signed or unsigned is implementation-defined; write signed char or unsigned char when the range matters.
sizeof(long) is 4 on 64-bit Windows but 8 on 64-bit Linux, so always fix the sizes before working out a sizeof answer.
A float keeps only about 7 significant digits, so a float and a double both set to 0.1 compare unequal; never test floating values with ==.

formulas.plainText: n-bit unsigned: 0 to 2^n - 1; n-bit signed: -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1
sizeof(char) = 1 <= sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long)
'A' = 65, so 'A' + 1 = 66 = 'B'; lowercase - uppercase = 32

notes.text: char stores the ASCII code: 'A' is 65, '0' is 48 and 'a' is 97, so 'A' + 1 == 66 == 'B' and '7' - '0' == 7. Printing a char with %d shows the code, with %c shows the character.
Integer division truncates: 5 / 2 == 2, but 5 % 2 == 1. Use 5.0 / 2 for 2.5. The same truncation happens when a double is stored in an int: int x = 7.9; gives 7.
#define takes no semicolon and no = sign: #define MAX = 100; replaces MAX with '= 100;' and breaks every use. A const variable does take both, and unlike a #define it has a type and a scope.
Local (auto) variables start with garbage, global and static variables start with 0. An MCQ that prints an uninitialised local has no defined answer; one that prints an uninitialised global prints 0.

formulas.title: Range of int
formulas.description: A 4-byte signed int in two's complement covers -2^31 to 2^31 - 1; unsigned int covers 0 to 2^32 - 1 = 4,294,967,295.

formulas.title: Range of an n-bit type
formulas.plainText: signed: -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1; unsigned: 0 to 2^n - 1
formulas.description: Works for every integer width: char (n = 8) gives -128 to 127 or 0 to 255, short (n = 16) gives -32,768 to 32,767 or 0 to 65,535.

formulas.title: Size ordering guarantee
formulas.plainText: sizeof(char) = 1 <= sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long)
formulas.description: The only sizes the standard fixes are the ordering and sizeof(char) = 1; the typical values are char 1, short 2, int 4, long 4 or 8, long long 8, float 4, double 8.

formulas.title: Character arithmetic
formulas.description: A char is a small integer holding an ASCII code, so characters can be added, compared and converted with plain arithmetic.

flashcards.front: Size of char, int, float and double on a typical 32-bit C compiler?
flashcards.back: char = 1 byte, int = 4 bytes, float = 4 bytes, double = 8 bytes (short = 2, long long = 8).

flashcards.front: What is a token, and what are the six kinds of tokens in C?
flashcards.back: The smallest unit the compiler recognises. Kinds: keywords (32 in ANSI C), identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and special symbols.

flashcards.front: How does const differ from #define?
flashcards.back: const creates a typed, scoped, read-only variable checked by the compiler; #define is a preprocessor text substitution with no type, no scope and no semicolon.

flashcards.front: What does a static local variable do?
flashcards.back: It is initialised once (to 0 by default), lives for the whole program run and keeps its value between calls of the function, unlike an auto local that is recreated on every call.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a keyword in C?
questions.explanation: main is an ordinary identifier: the name of the function where execution starts. volatile, extern and register are all among the 32 keywords of ANSI C.

questions.questionText: Which of the following keywords was added by C99 and is NOT one of the 32 keywords of ANSI C (C89)?
questions.explanation: C99 added inline, restrict, _Bool, _Complex and _Imaginary. volatile, signed and enum were already in the C89 list of 32 keywords.

questions.questionText: Which of the following declarations compiles without error in C?
questions.explanation: Keywords are all lowercase and C is case-sensitive, so Default is an ordinary identifier. sizeof, goto and typedef are reserved keywords and cannot be used as variable names.

questions.questionText:
How many of the following are valid C identifiers?

net_pay   _count   2ndValue   float   Float   pay-rate   rate2
questions.explanation: Valid: net_pay, _count, Float and rate2. 2ndValue starts with a digit, float is a keyword (Float is not, because case matters) and pay-rate contains a hyphen, which is read as pay minus rate.

questions.questionText: In C, the names total, Total and TOTAL:
options: all refer to the same variable
are invalid because identifiers must be lowercase
are the same identifier unless they are declared in different files
questions.explanation: C is case-sensitive, so identifiers that differ only in letter case are distinct; declaring all three creates three separate variables.
A leading 0 means octal and 0x means hexadecimal: 017 = 1 × 8 + 7 = 15, 0x17 = 1 × 16 + 7 = 23, and 17 is plain decimal.

questions.questionText: Which integer constant has the type unsigned long long?
questions.explanation: U makes a constant unsigned and LL makes it long long, so 25ULL (also written 25LLU) is unsigned long long. 25UL is unsigned long, 25LL is long long and 25U is unsigned int.
5LL is a long long (8 bytes) and 5.0f is a float (4 bytes). A character constant such as '5' has type int in C, so sizeof('5') is 4 (it would be 1 in C++).

options: Compile error: 2147483648 is too large for int
questions.explanation: In C99 and later, an unsuffixed decimal constant gets the first of int, long, long long that can hold it. 2147483647 = 2^31 - 1 fits in a 4-byte int; 2147483648 = 2^31 fits neither int nor a 4-byte long, so it becomes long long (8 bytes). (Under the old C89 rules it would have been unsigned long, 4 bytes.)

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a valid floating-point constant in C?
questions.explanation: 1.5e-3 means 1.5 × 10^-3 = 0.0015. An exponent needs digits after the e, commas are not allowed inside a number, and e3 with no digits in front is an identifier, not a constant.

The literal holds A, a tab (from \t), B, one backslash (from \\) and the letter n, so strlen gives 5. The \\ pair is a single backslash, so the n that follows is an ordinary letter, not part of a newline.
\101 is octal 101 = 1 × 64 + 0 × 8 + 1 = 65 = 'A' and \x42 is hex 42 = 66 = 'B'. The array holds 'A', 'B' and the terminating '\0', so sizeof is 3 while %s prints AB.

questions.questionText: Which escape sequence moves the output to the next horizontal tab stop?
questions.explanation: \t is the horizontal tab. \b is backspace, \v is vertical tab and \r is carriage return (back to the start of the current line).
Character constants are small integers holding ASCII codes: '\n' (line feed) is 10, '\0' (the null character) is 0 and the digit character '0' is 48. 13 would be '\r'.

An octal escape uses at most three octal digits, so \123 (1 × 64 + 2 × 8 + 3 = 83 = 'S') is one character and the 4 after it is an ordinary character. The string is S4 and strlen, which does not count the '\0', is 2.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a derived data type in C?
questions.explanation: Derived types are built from other types: arrays, pointers and functions. int, char and double are fundamental (primary) data types.

questions.questionText: Which statement about void is correct in standard C?
options: A void * pointer can hold the address of any object, but it must be converted to a typed pointer before it is dereferenced
A variable can be declared with type void so that it can hold a value of any type
A function declared to return void must end with return 0;
questions.explanation: void means no value: it is used as a return type, for an empty parameter list and for generic pointers. No object can have type void, sizeof(void) is not allowed in standard C (1 is only a GCC extension), and a void function returns nothing.

questions.questionText: An unsigned char occupies 8 bits. What range of values can it hold?
questions.explanation: With n = 8 bits an unsigned type covers 0 to 2^n - 1 = 2^8 - 1 = 255. The range -128 to 127 belongs to a signed char.

questions.questionText: Assume short is 16 bits and uses two's complement. What are the minimum value of a signed short and the maximum value of an unsigned short?

questions.explanation: c + 10 is computed in int as 260; storing it back in an 8-bit unsigned char reduces it modulo 2^8: 260 - 256 = 4. Unsigned values wrap round, they never stop at 255.
Unsigned arithmetic is done modulo 2^32: 3 - 5 = -2, and -2 + 4,294,967,296 = 4,294,967,294. An unsigned result can never be negative.

questions.questionText: What do the modifiers signed and unsigned change when applied to int?
options: The number of bytes, but not the range of values
Both the number of bytes and the range of values
Only the way printf displays the value
The range of values, but not the number of bytes
questions.explanation: sizeof(unsigned int) equals sizeof(int); only the range moves. A 4-byte int covers -2^31 to 2^31 - 1 and a 4-byte unsigned int covers 0 to 2^32 - 1. short and long are the modifiers that change the size.

questions.questionText: Which declaration is NOT valid in standard C?
questions.explanation: long may modify int and double, but long float is not a C type (it was an early K&R spelling of double). long double, short int and unsigned long long are all standard types.

const int *p is a pointer to a read-only int: p may be pointed elsewhere, but *p cannot be changed through p. int *const q is a constant pointer: *q may be changed, but q cannot be re-pointed. a itself is not const.

questions.questionText: The volatile qualifier on a variable tells the compiler that:
options: it should be kept in a CPU register for faster access
it cannot be modified after it is initialised
it is defined in another source file
its value may change outside the program's visible code, so every access must really read or write memory
questions.explanation: volatile is used for hardware registers, signal handlers and shared memory: the compiler must not cache the value or remove reads and writes that look redundant. register asks for register storage, const forbids modification and extern refers to another file.

options: It compiles but crashes at run time
questions.explanation: A const variable may be given a value only in its initialisation. The later assignment max = 20 is a constraint violation, so the compiler rejects the program.

questions.questionText: In standard C (C11), which of the following may be used as a case label in a switch statement?
options: A const int variable such as K, declared as const int K = 2;
An enumeration constant such as RED
questions.explanation: A case label must be an integer constant expression. An enumeration constant is one; a const int variable is not a constant expression in C (it is in C++, and some C compilers accept it only as an extension), and floating constants and strings are not integers.
s is static, so it is initialised once and grows 5 -> 7 -> 9 -> 11 over the three calls, while the automatic a restarts at 5 each time and ends at 7. The third call returns 11 × 10 + 7 = 117.

Inside f the static local x hides the global x; it starts at 1 and doubles on each call, so a = 2 and b = 4. The block's own x = 3 gives a = 2 + 3 = 5 and vanishes at the closing brace, so printf sees the global x = 10.

questions.questionText: Which operation is NOT allowed on a variable declared as register int r = 5; in C?
options: Using it in a loop condition
questions.explanation: The address of a register variable may not be taken in C, because the value may live in a CPU register that has no memory address. Ordinary reads, writes and increments are allowed.

questions.questionText: What does the declaration extern int count; written at file scope do?
options: It defines count and initialises it to 0
It makes count visible only inside the current file
It creates a separate copy of count for each function
It declares count without allocating storage; the definition must be in some file of the program
questions.explanation: extern announces a global variable that is defined elsewhere, usually in another .c file, so the linker can connect the uses to that one definition; no storage is reserved by the declaration itself.

questions.questionText: A global variable is declared as static int hits; in file a.c. Which statement about hits is correct?
options: It can be used from b.c after writing extern int hits; there
It is re-initialised whenever a function in a.c is called
It can be used only by code in a.c
It is stored on the stack
questions.explanation: static at file scope gives internal linkage: the name is private to a.c, so an extern declaration in b.c cannot reach it. It still lives for the whole run in the data segment and starts at 0.

questions.questionText: What is the default storage class of a variable declared inside a function without any storage-class keyword?
questions.explanation: Local variables are auto by default: they are created when the block is entered, destroyed when it is left, and hold garbage until they are assigned.

options: Compile error: the variables are not initialised
questions.explanation: Objects with static storage duration (globals, static globals and static locals) are set to zero before the program starts, so all three print 0. Only automatic locals start with garbage.
s is static, so it is initialised once and doubles on every pass: 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 30. a is automatic and restarts at 1 each pass, adding 2 × 4 = 8. total = 30 + 8 = 38.
An enumerator without a value is one more than the previous one: LOW = 2 so MID = 3; HIGH is set to 10 so MAX = 11. HIGH - LOW = 10 - 2 = 8.
Counting on from A = -2 gives B = -1 and C = 0. D = A + 5 = -2 + 5 = 3 and E = 4, so E + B = 4 + (-1) = 3.
STR is a real type name for char *, so a and b are both pointers (8 bytes). PSTR is plain text replacement: PSTR c, d; becomes char * c, d; so only c is a pointer and d is a char (1 byte).

questions.questionText: What does typedef unsigned long ulong; do?
options: It makes ulong another name for the type unsigned long
It declares a variable named ulong of type unsigned long
It creates a new type that cannot be mixed with unsigned long
It tells the preprocessor to replace the text ulong everywhere
questions.explanation: typedef gives an existing type an alias and allocates no storage; ulong x; now means unsigned long x;. It is handled by the compiler, not the preprocessor, and the alias is fully compatible with the original type.
Row is an alias for "array of 4 int", so sizeof(Row) = 4 × 4 = 16 bytes. m is an array of 3 such rows (the same as int m[3][4]), so sizeof(m) = 3 × 16 = 48 bytes.
Converting any non-zero value to _Bool gives 1 and converting zero gives 0, so b = 1 and z = 0. In b + b both operands are promoted to int, so n = 1 + 1 = 2.

options: Compile error: a float cannot be compared with a double
The output changes from run to run
questions.explanation: 0.1 has no exact binary form. The float keeps about 7 significant digits and the double about 16, so when f is converted to double for the comparison it is 0.100000001490116..., which differs from the double 0.1000000000000000055...
'A' is 65, so c = 67, which is the code of 'C', and d = 68 = 'D'. %c prints the character and %d prints its numeric code.

subtopics.title: Operators & Precedence
subtopics.subtitle: Operator groups, pre/post increment, precedence, type promotion and short-circuit

concepts.text: Operator Groups
C operators by category (unary operators take one operand, binary two, and ?: is the only ternary operator):
items: Arithmetic: + - * / % (modulus works on integers only; / on two integers truncates toward zero).
Relational: < > <= >= == != (the result is an int, 1 for true and 0 for false).
Logical: && || ! (operands are any scalar; result is 1 or 0; && and || short-circuit).
Bitwise: & | ^ ~ << >> (integer operands, operate on individual bits).
Assignment: = and the compound forms += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= (a += b means a = a + (b)).
Increment/decrement: ++x (pre: change first, then use) vs x++ (post: use first, then change).
Conditional: cond ? a : b, an expression form of if/else that evaluates only one branch.
Comma: evaluates left to right and yields the rightmost value; sizeof: compile-time size in bytes; (type): explicit cast.
Others: & address-of, * dereference, [] subscript, () call, . and -> member access.

concepts.text: Pre vs Post Increment

int x = 5, y = 5;
int a = ++x;   /* x becomes 6 first, then a = 6 (pre-increment) */
int b = y++;   /* b gets 5, then y becomes 6 (post-increment)   */
printf("%d %d %d %d\n", a, x, b, y);   /* 6 6 5 6 */

int n = 10;
printf("%d\n", n++ * 2);   /* 20: old value used, n is now 11 */
printf("%d\n", ++n * 2);   /* 24: n becomes 12 first */
printf("%d\n", n);         /* 12 */

Pre-increment changes the variable and yields the new value; post-increment yields the old value and then changes the variable. As a statement on its own, i++; and ++i; do exactly the same thing. Both forms need a modifiable variable (an lvalue), so 5++ and (a + b)++ are compile errors. Modifying the same variable twice in one expression without a sequence point, such as i++ + ++i or a[i] = i++, is undefined behaviour: different compilers print different numbers, so 'undefined' is the only defensible answer.
Precedence and Associativity

rows: Right to left (comma: left to right)

concepts.text: Reading the table in practice:
items: Multiplicative before additive: 2 + 3 * 4 = 14, and 10 - 4 - 3 = 3 because - is left-associative ((10 - 4) - 3).
Unary minus binds tighter than *: -a * b is (-a) * b; sizeof x + 1 is (sizeof x) + 1.
Relational beats equality beats logical: a < b == c < d parses as (a < b) == (c < d); a || b && c is a || (b && c).
Bitwise & ^ | sit BELOW == and !=, so x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0) = x & 0 = 0. Always write (x & 1) == 0.
Assignment is right-to-left: a = b = c = 5 assigns 5 to all three; x = y == z stores the comparison result in x.
The comma has the lowest precedence: x = 1, 2, 3; leaves x = 1, while x = (1, 2, 3); gives x = 3.
Parentheses override everything; when in doubt in an MCQ, rebuild the expression with brackets level by level.

concepts.text: Arithmetic Details, Promotion and Casting
Integer division and modulus:
items: 7 / 2 = 3 and 7 / 2.0 = 3.5: one floating operand makes the whole division floating.
C99 truncates toward zero: -7 / 2 = -3 (not -4), and the sign of a % b follows the dividend a: -7 % 2 = -1, 7 % -2 = 1, 5 % -3 = 2.
The identity (a / b) * b + a % b == a always holds; a % b == 0 tests divisibility.
% is not defined for float or double (compile error); use fmod() from math.h.
1 / 2 * 4 = 0 because 1 / 2 is evaluated first as 0; 1 / 2.0 * 4 = 2.0. Division by zero with integers is undefined behaviour (usually a crash).

concepts.text: Implicit conversion (usual arithmetic conversions) and casts:
items: Integer promotion: char and short operands are promoted to int before any arithmetic, so 'A' + 1 is an int.
In a mixed expression the 'smaller' type is converted to the larger: int -> unsigned -> long -> float -> double -> long double.
Mixing signed and unsigned converts the signed value: -1 < 1u is FALSE because -1 becomes 4294967295.
Assignment converts the right side to the type of the left: int i = 3.9; stores 3; float f = 1 / 3; stores 0.0 (integer division happened first).
A cast (type)expr converts explicitly: (float)a / b gives the fractional quotient, (int)3.9 gives 3 (truncation), (char)65 is 'A'.
sizeof(a + 1.5) is 8 because the expression has type double; sizeof never evaluates its operand, so sizeof(i++) leaves i unchanged.

concepts.text:
int a = 7, b = 2;
float f = a / b;                     /* 3.0: integer division happens FIRST */
float g = (float)a / b;              /* 3.5: cast before the division */
printf("%d %d\n", -7 / 2, -7 % 2);  /* -3 -1 */
printf("%d\n", 5 % -3);             /* 2: sign follows the dividend (5) */
printf("%d\n", -1 < 1u);            /* 0: -1 converts to unsigned */
printf("%d\n", 10 / 3 * 3.0 == 10); /* 0: 10/3 = 3, 3 * 3.0 = 9.0 */
printf("%d\n", (int)(3.7 + 0.5));   /* 4: cheap rounding trick */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(a + 1.5));   /* 8: expression is a double */
Logical, Bitwise, Conditional and Comma
Short-circuit evaluation and bitwise facts:
items: && stops at the first false operand and || at the first true one, so if (p != NULL && *p > 0) never dereferences a NULL pointer.
Skipped operands are not evaluated, side effects included: x = 0; y = x && ++x; leaves x = 0 and y = 0.
Logical operators return exactly 0 or 1: !5 = 0, !0 = 1, !!7 = 1, 2 && 4 = 1, 0 || 3 = 1.
x << n multiplies by 2^n and x >> n divides by 2^n for non-negative x; x & 1 tests odd, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x (basis of the XOR swap).
2 & 4 = 0 but 2 && 4 = 1; & is bitwise, && is logical: the single most common mix-up in output questions.
?: evaluates only the chosen branch: max = (a > b) ? a : b; it can be nested and chained like an else-if ladder.

concepts.text: sizeof is an operator, not a function, and its result is a size_t (print with %zu or cast to int). On a typical 32-bit-int system sizeof(int) is 4, sizeof(3.0) is 8, sizeof(3.0f) is 4, sizeof('A') is 4 in C but 1 in C++, and sizeof of an array is the whole array in bytes. Because sizeof is evaluated at compile time from the type alone, sizeof(i++) leaves i unchanged and sizeof(x)/sizeof(x[0]) counts array elements.
Going Deeper: Evaluating Expressions Step by Step

Precedence and associativity decide only how an expression is grouped, not the order in which its operands are computed. In a + b * c the multiplication is grouped first, but the compiler may fetch a, b and c in any order. Only four operators promise to finish their left operand first: &&, ||, ?: and the comma operator. Everywhere else, if a side effect (++, -- or an embedded assignment) changes a variable that another part of the same expression also reads or changes, as in i++ + i, the behaviour is undefined. A plain i = i + 1 is fine, because the store happens only after the right side has been computed.

flashcards.front: Difference between == and = in C?
flashcards.back: == compares two values and yields 1 or 0; = assigns the right value to the left variable and yields that value. Using = inside a condition is a classic bug.

flashcards.front: With int a = 5; what do a++ and ++a each evaluate to, and what is a afterwards?
flashcards.back: a++ evaluates to 5 (old value), ++a evaluates to 6 (new value); in both cases a is 6 afterwards.

flashcards.front: What is short-circuit evaluation?
flashcards.back: && stops evaluating as soon as an operand is false and || as soon as one is true; the remaining operands, including their side effects such as ++, are never evaluated.

flashcards.front: In what order are * / %, + -, relational, ==, &&, || and = applied?
flashcards.back: Highest to lowest: * / % then + - then < <= > >= then == != then && then || then = (assignment is right-to-left). Parentheses override all of them.

questions.explanation: Both operands are int, so 17 / 5 = 3.4 is truncated to 3. The remainder is 17 % 5 = 17 - 3 × 5 = 2.

C99 and C11 truncate the quotient toward zero (C89 left this implementation-defined), so -17 / 5 = -3.4 -> -3 (not -4). The remainder follows a % b = a - (a / b) × b: -17 - (-3 × 5) = -2 and 17 - (-3 × -5) = 2, so it takes the sign of the dividend.

questions.questionText: Which of the following expressions causes a compile error in C?
questions.explanation: The % operator requires integer operands; a floating-point remainder needs fmod() from <math.h>. The other three are legal and give 1, -1 and 3.5.
a / b * b groups left to right in int arithmetic: 9 / 4 = 2, then 2 × 4 = 8. The cast binds tighter than /, so (double)a / b = 9.0 / 4 = 2.25. r = 8 + 2.25 = 10.25.
* / % share one precedence level and group left to right: n % 10 = 9, n / 10 % 10 = 472 % 10 = 2 and n / 100 % 10 = 47 % 10 = 7. s = 9 + 2 + 7 = 18.
Relational, equality and logical operators produce an int: 1 for true and 0 for false. 5 > 3 is 1, 5 == 3 is 0 and !(5 < 3) is !0 = 1.
== groups left to right and yields 0 or 1: a == b == c is (a == b) == c = 1 == 5 = 0, while a == b == 1 is (5 == 5) == 1 = 1 == 1 = 1. C never reads a chain of comparisons the mathematical way.
i++ > 0 compares the old value 0, so it is false, and i becomes 1. Because the left side of || is false, the right side must be evaluated: j becomes 6 and 6 > 5 is true, so r = 1.

&& binds tighter than ||, so r = (a-- && b++) || ++c. a-- yields 1 (a becomes 0), so b++ is evaluated: it yields 0 (b becomes 1) and the && is false. The || therefore evaluates ++c, giving c = 6 (true), so r = 1.
&& has higher precedence, so the expression is x || (++y && ++y). x = 4 is true, so || stops at once: neither ++y runs, y stays 0, and z = 1 because logical operators produce 1, not the value 4.

questions.questionText: In C, what does a relational or logical expression such as a < b or a && b evaluate to?
options: A bool whose value is true or false
An int that may be any non-zero value when true
An int whose value is 1 (true) or 0 (false)
questions.explanation: C operators such as <, ==, && and ! give an int that is exactly 1 or 0. Any non-zero value counts as true when it is tested, but these operators always produce 1 for true.
12 = 1100 and 10 = 1010 in binary. AND keeps the common 1s: 1000 = 8; OR keeps every 1: 1110 = 14; XOR keeps the bits that differ: 0110 = 6.
x << n multiplies by 2^n: 3 × 2^4 = 48. x >> n divides a non-negative value by 2^n and drops the remainder: 100 / 8 = 12.5 -> 12.
In two's complement ~x = -x - 1, so ~12 = -12 - 1 = -13 and ~(-12) = 12 - 1 = 11. Flipping only the four bits of 1100 to get 0011 = 3 forgets that an int has 32 bits.
== has higher precedence than &, so the condition is x & (2 == 2) = 6 & 1 = 110 & 001 = 0, which is false. Writing (x & 2) == 2 would print yes.
Additive operators bind tighter than shifts, so the expression is 1 << (2 + 3) = 1 << 5 = 32, not (1 << 2) + 3 = 7.
0x5A = 0101 1010. f |= 1 sets bit 0: 0101 1011 (0x5B). f &= ~(1u << 4) clears bit 4: 0100 1011 (0x4B). f ^= 1u << 7 flips bit 7 from 0 to 1: 1100 1011 = 0xCB, printed by %X as CB.
Step by step: 10 + 5 = 15, 15 × 2 = 30, 30 - 4 = 26, and 26 / 3 = 8 because both operands are int.
A compound assignment evaluates its whole right side first: a *= 2 + 3 means a = a * (2 + 3) = 4 × 5 = 20, not a * 2 + 3 = 11.
x = 5 is an assignment, not a comparison: it stores 5 in x and the value of the expression, 5, is non-zero (true), so the if branch prints A 5.

questions.questionText: Given int x = 1, y = 2; which of the following statements causes a compile error?
questions.explanation: The left operand of an assignment must be a modifiable lvalue such as a variable. x + 1 is a computed value with no storage, so it cannot be assigned to. The others are a chained assignment, a chained compound assignment and a comma expression.
Assignment operators group right to left: a += (b *= (c -= 1)). First c = 4 - 1 = 3, then b = 3 × 3 = 9, then a = 2 + 9 = 11.
Post-decrement hands the old value 8 to the expression, so n = 8 - 3 = 5; afterwards m is 7.
++i increments first and yields 4; j-- yields the old value 3 and then j becomes 2. k = 4 × 3 = 12.
Each test uses the old i and then increments it. The tests 0, 1, 2 and 3 < 4 succeed and add the new values 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The failing test 4 < 4 still increments i, so i ends at 5.
The compiler always takes the longest possible token (maximal munch), so x+++y is read as (x++) + y: z = 5 + 2 = 7, x then becomes 6 and y is unchanged.

questions.questionText: When i++; and ++i; are each used as a complete statement on its own, how do they differ?
options: They have the same effect: each adds 1 to i
i++; leaves i unchanged and only ++i; increments it
++i; is not allowed as a stand-alone statement
They differ only when i is a float
questions.explanation: The difference between pre- and post-increment is only in the value the expression yields. When that value is not used, both simply add 1 to i.

options: The behaviour is undefined, because i is modified more than once without sequencing
questions.explanation: ++i, i++ and the assignment all modify i with no sequence point between them, so the behaviour is undefined and different compilers may print different values. Only output questions that modify each variable once per expression have a defined answer.
7 % 2 is 1, which is non-zero (true), so the conditional operator selects its second operand, the string "odd".
?: groups right to left, so the chain works like an else-if ladder: 65 >= 80 is false, 65 >= 60 is true, so g = 'B' and the remaining tests are never evaluated.
3 > 7 is false, so only the third operand b-- is evaluated: c receives the old value 7 and b becomes 6. The a++ in the unchosen branch never runs, so a stays 3.
?: has lower precedence than +, so y = x > 3 ? 10 : (20 + 1) = 10. In z the parentheses finish the conditional first, giving 10 + 1 = 11.
The comma operator evaluates left to right and yields its last operand: a += 3 makes a = 5, a * 2 is computed and thrown away, and a - 1 = 4 is stored in b.

Assignment binds more tightly than the comma operator, so x = a++, b + a; means (x = a++), (b + a): x gets 2, a becomes 3 and the value of b + a is thrown away. In y = (a++, b + a) the parentheses make the whole comma expression the value assigned; a becomes 4 before b + a is evaluated, so y = 5 + 4 = 9.
In c + 1 the char is promoted to int, so the size is 4. c = 'B' has the type of c (char, size 1), but sizeof never evaluates its operand, so the assignment never happens and c is still 'A'.

questions.questionText: Which statement about sizeof in C is correct?
options: It is a library function declared in <stdlib.h>
It is a preprocessor directive like #define
It returns the number of elements of any array passed to a function
It is a unary operator, normally worked out at compile time, that gives a size in bytes
questions.explanation: sizeof is a keyword operator that the compiler evaluates from the type of its operand (only variable-length arrays need run time), and its result has type size_t. Parentheses are required only around a type name, as in sizeof(int).

options: Compile error: signed and unsigned cannot be compared
questions.explanation: When an int meets an unsigned int, the int is converted to unsigned: -5 becomes 2^32 - 5 = 4,294,967,291, which is not less than 3, so the else branch runs.
Integer promotion converts both char operands to int before the addition, so 100 + 100 = 200 is computed in int and stored in the int s without any overflow.
Converting a floating value to int discards the fraction (truncation toward zero, not rounding down): (int)-3.7 = -3, (int)3.7 = 3 and (int)-0.5 = 0, so the second value is 3 + 0 = 3.
In u + i the int -3 is converted to unsigned, and the sum is taken modulo 2^32: 2 - 3 = -1 -> 4,294,967,295. That unsigned value is greater than 5, so the comparison gives 1.

questions.questionText: Given the declarations int i; float f; double d;, what is the type of the expression i * f + d?
questions.explanation: By the usual arithmetic conversions, i * f is computed as float, and float + double is computed as double, so the whole expression has type double.
* / % have equal precedence and group left to right: 3 * 4 = 12, 12 % 5 = 2 and 6 / 4 = 1 in integer division. Then 2 + 2 - 1 = 3.
From high to low the levels used are +, <<, &, |. So 1 + 2 = 3, 3 << 1 = 6, 6 & 7 = 6, and finally 8 | 6 = 1000 | 0110 = 1110 = 14. Reading strictly left to right would give 6.

questions.questionText: Which group of C operators associates from right to left?
options: Unary operators, the conditional operator ?: and the assignment operators
The logical operators && and || and the comma operator
questions.explanation: Unary operators (such as !, ~, prefix ++ and casts), ?: and every assignment operator group right to left, so a = b = c assigns c to b first. Almost all binary operators, including the comma, group left to right.

questions.questionText: Which of the following operators has the LOWEST precedence in C?
questions.explanation: The comma operator is at the very bottom of the precedence table, below the assignment operators, which are below ?:, which in turn is below ||.

subtopics.subtitle: printf/scanf specifiers, width and precision, input-buffer pitfalls, getchar/gets/fgets

concepts.text: Streams and the Two Kinds of I/O

All standard input and output in C goes through streams declared in stdio.h: stdin (keyboard, buffered until Enter), stdout (screen, line-buffered) and stderr (screen, unbuffered, for error messages). Formatted I/O uses a format string containing conversion specifiers to translate between text and typed values: printf and scanf on the console, fprintf/fscanf on files, sprintf/sscanf on strings. Unformatted I/O moves raw characters or whole lines with no conversion: getchar/putchar, gets/puts, fgets/fputs, and the non-standard getch/getche from conio.h.
printf and the Format Specifiers

rows: double (printf promotes float to double, so %f works for both; scanf needs %f for float and %lf for double)
pointer address / a literal percent sign

concepts.text: Flags, field width and precision go between % and the letter: %[flags][width][.precision][length]specifier.
items: %5d right-justifies in 5 columns ('   42'); %-5d left-justifies ('42   '); %05d pads with zeros ('00042'); %+d always shows the sign (+42).
%.2f rounds to two decimals (3.14159 -> 3.14); %8.3f uses width 8 and 3 decimals ('   3.142'); the default precision of %f is 6.
%.3s prints only the first 3 characters of a string; %10s right-aligns a string in 10 columns; %-10s left-aligns it.
%*d takes the width from the next argument: printf("%*d", 6, 42) prints 42 in 6 columns.
%e prints 3.141590e+00; %g uses the shorter of %e and %f and drops trailing zeros (3.14).
A width smaller than the value never truncates a number: %2d with 12345 still prints 12345.
printf returns the number of characters printed; scanf returns the number of items successfully converted (EOF on end of input).

int n = 42; double pi = 3.14159; char s[] = "exam";
printf("[%d]\n", n);          /* [42]       */
printf("[%5d]\n", n);         /* [   42]    */
printf("[%-5d]\n", n);        /* [42   ]    */
printf("[%05d]\n", n);        /* [00042]    */
printf("[%.2f]\n", pi);       /* [3.14]     */
printf("[%8.3f]\n", pi);      /* [   3.142] */
printf("[%s|%.2s]\n", s, s);  /* [exam|ex]  */
printf("[%x %o %c]\n", 255, 8, 65);   /* [ff 10 A] */
printf("%d\n", printf("hi"));  /* prints hi2: printf returns 2 */
scanf: Reading Formatted Input
scanf rules that produce most of the bugs (and MCQs):
items: Every non-array argument must be an address: scanf("%d", &n). Forgetting & compiles (maybe with a warning) and crashes or corrupts memory at run time.
An array or string name is already an address, so scanf("%s", name) takes no &.
%s skips leading whitespace and stops at the next whitespace, so it cannot read 'New Delhi'; use %[^\n] or fgets for a whole line, and give a bound like %29s to avoid overflow.
%d, %f and %s skip leading whitespace, but %c reads ANY character including the newline left by a previous Enter; write " %c" (leading space) to skip whitespace first.
%f reads a float and %lf reads a double: unlike printf, mixing them here is a real bug because the wrong number of bytes is written.
scanf returns the count of items converted (2 for "%d %d" on success) or EOF; a non-numeric character stops %d and stays in the buffer, so later reads fail repeatedly.
Input is line-buffered: nothing reaches scanf until Enter is pressed, and the '\n' itself remains in the buffer after a number is read.

concepts.text:
int age, a, b; char grade; char name[30];
scanf("%d", &age);        /* user types 21<Enter>: '\n' stays in the buffer */
scanf("%c", &grade);      /* reads that leftover '\n', NOT the letter!       */
scanf(" %c", &grade);     /* leading space skips whitespace: works           */
scanf("%s", name);        /* no &: name is already an address; stops at space */
scanf("%29[^\n]", name);  /* reads a whole line, at most 29 characters       */
int items = scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);  /* 2 on success, 0/1 on bad input, EOF at end */
Unformatted I/O Functions

rows: Read / write one character on stdin / stdout; getchar returns an int (EOF = -1) and waits for Enter because stdin is buffered
Read a line into s with NO length check (buffer overflow; removed in C11) / write s followed by a newline
Safe line read of at most n-1 characters (keeps the '\n' if it fits) / write s with no extra newline
Read a key immediately without Enter; getch does not echo, getche echoes the key
Character I/O on any stream; getc(stdin) is the same as getchar()
Formatted output into / input from a character array instead of a stream

concepts.text:
char line[50];
int ch = getchar();                 /* waits for Enter; returns an int */
putchar(ch);                        /* echo it */
putchar('\n');
gets(line);                         /* UNSAFE: no bound; never use */
fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin);    /* safe; keeps the '\n' if it fits */
puts(line);                         /* adds its own '\n' */
fputs(line, stdout);                /* prints exactly line, no newline added */
Formatted vs unformatted at a glance:
items: Formatted: printf/scanf family; converts numbers of any type using specifiers; flexible but slower because the format string is parsed at run time.
Unformatted: getchar/putchar, gets/puts, fgets/fputs, getch/getche; raw characters and strings only, no conversion, faster.
puts("Hi") is equivalent to printf("Hi\n") and printf("%s\n", s); putchar('A') is equivalent to printf("%c", 'A').
getchar/scanf wait for Enter (buffered); getch/getche return at once (unbuffered) but are not part of standard C or gcc on Linux.
printf returns the number of characters written, scanf the number of items read, getchar the character as an int or EOF, gets/fgets a pointer or NULL.

concepts.text: Output buffering matters too. stdout is line-buffered when attached to a terminal, so a printf without \n may not appear until a newline is printed, fflush(stdout) is called, or the program ends. fflush(stdin) is undefined behaviour in standard C (it happens to work on some Windows compilers); the portable way to discard leftover input is a loop such as while ((c = getchar()) != '\n' && c != EOF);. stderr is unbuffered, so fprintf(stderr, "...") appears immediately, which is why error messages go there.

Going Deeper: Flags, %g, scanf Controls and String I/O

printf walks through its format string from left to right. Ordinary characters are copied unchanged, and each conversion consumes the next argument, which must have exactly the type the specifier expects; a mismatch (such as an int passed to %f) or a missing argument is undefined behaviour, while surplus arguments are evaluated and ignored. A conversion first produces its natural text and only then applies the width, so each field contributes max(width, natural length) characters. Adding these lengths and the ordinary characters gives printf's return value.

rows: Left-justify inside the field (pad on the right)
Pad numbers with leading zeros; ignored with -, and for integers when a precision is given
Always print a sign for signed conversions
Print a blank where a + would go; ignored if + is also present
Alternate form: 0 prefix for %o, 0x or 0X for %x/%X, keep the point for %f/%e and trailing zeros for %g

concepts.plainText: each field prints max(width, natural length) characters; printf returns the sum of the field lengths plus the literal characters

concepts.text: How %g chooses between fixed and exponential style (P = precision, default 6; X = the exponent the value would have in %e style):
items: If P > X >= -4, %g uses fixed style with P - 1 - X decimals; otherwise it uses e-style with P - 1 decimals.
Trailing zeros, and a decimal point left at the end, are then removed unless the # flag is given.
100000.0 has X = 5, so it prints 100000; 1000000.0 has X = 6, so it prints 1e+06.
0.0001234 has X = -4 and stays fixed (0.0001234); 0.00001234 has X = -5 and prints 1.234e-05.
%.3g keeps 3 significant digits: 1234.0 prints 1.23e+03 and 3.14159 prints 3.14.
%e and %g always print at least two exponent digits, as in e+05 or e-12.

concepts.text: scanf controls that go beyond the basic rules:
items: A width limits one conversion: with input 12345, "%2d%d" stores 12 and 345.
An asterisk suppresses assignment: %*d reads a number and discards it, and it is not counted in the return value.
%i reads integers the way C constants are written (010 is octal 8, 0x10 is hexadecimal 16), whereas %d always reads decimal.
A scanset reads characters from a set: %[a-z] takes lowercase letters only and %[^,] takes everything up to a comma; always add a width such as %19[^,].
Whitespace in the format matches any amount of whitespace, including none; any other character must match the input exactly, or scanf stops and returns the count so far.
%n stores the number of characters consumed so far into an int and is not counted in the return value.
