printf returns the number of characters written; scanf returns the number of items converted (or EOF)
%f prints 6 decimals by default; %.nf rounds to n decimals

notes.text: In scanf the length modifier matters: %f for float, %lf for double, %ld for long, %c for char. In printf a float is promoted to double, so %f prints both; %lf is merely tolerated there.
scanf("%d", n) without & passes the VALUE of n as an address: it compiles but crashes or corrupts memory. Only arrays and strings are passed without & because their name is already an address.
After scanf("%d", &n) the Enter key's '\n' is still in the input buffer, so a following getchar() or scanf("%c", &ch) reads the newline instead of waiting. Use " %c" or consume the newline first.
gets() cannot limit how many characters it stores, so any long line overflows the array; it was removed from C11. Use fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin) and remember it keeps the trailing '\n'.

formulas.title: Format specifier syntax
formulas.plainText: %[flags][width][.precision][length]specifier
formulas.description: Flags (-, +, 0, space, #), a minimum field width, a precision after the dot, a length modifier (l, ll, h) and finally the conversion letter (d i u f e g c s x o p).

formulas.title: fgets bound
formulas.plainText: fgets(s, n, stdin) stores at most n - 1 characters plus '\0'
formulas.description: The size argument makes fgets safe where gets is not; the newline is kept if it fits, so strip it with s[strcspn(s, "\n")] = 0 if needed.

formulas.title: Return values of printf and scanf
formulas.plainText: printf returns characters written; scanf returns items converted (or EOF)
formulas.description: printf("%d", printf("hi")) prints hi2, and checking scanf's return is the only way to detect bad input.

formulas.title: Default precision of %f
formulas.plainText: %f prints 6 decimals; %.2f prints 2 decimals (rounded)
formulas.description: printf("%f", 3.14) prints 3.140000, printf("%.2f", 3.14159) prints 3.14 and printf("%.0f", 2.5) prints 2 (round-half-even in glibc).

flashcards.front: Difference between getch() and getche()?
flashcards.back: Both read a key immediately without waiting for Enter (conio.h, non-standard); getch does not echo the key on screen, getche echoes it.

flashcards.front: Why does scanf("%d", &n) need & but scanf("%s", name) does not?
flashcards.back: scanf writes through addresses; &n gives the address of n, while an array name such as name already evaluates to the address of its first element.

flashcards.front: What does printf("%d", printf("NEC")) print?
flashcards.back: NEC3. The inner printf prints NEC and returns 3 (characters written), which the outer printf then prints.

flashcards.front: Why prefer fgets over gets?
flashcards.back: gets has no length limit, so long input overflows the array (removed in C11); fgets(s, n, stdin) reads at most n - 1 characters and keeps the trailing newline.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%-5d|%05.1f]", 42, 3.14159);
questions.explanation: %-5d left-justifies 42 in a 5-column field, giving '42   '. %05.1f rounds to one decimal (3.1) and zero-pads to a width of 5, giving '003.1'.

options: '\n' (the newline left in the input buffer)
questions.explanation: scanf("%d") consumes the digits 25 but leaves the Enter key's newline in the buffer; getchar() then returns that '\n' immediately instead of waiting for new input.

questions.questionText:
Assume the ASCII character set. What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%d %c %x", 'A', 66, 255);
questions.explanation: In C a character constant such as 'A' has type int, so %d prints its code 65. %c prints the character whose code is 66 (B), and %x prints 255 in lowercase hexadecimal, ff.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%.3f", 2.0 / 3);
questions.explanation: 2.0 / 3 is a double division giving 0.666666...; %.3f keeps three decimals and rounds using the next digit (6), so 0.667 is printed.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%6s][%-6s]", "Kath", "Kath");
questions.explanation: A width of 6 for a 4-letter string adds 2 spaces: on the left by default (right-justified), and on the right when the - flag is given (left-justified).

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%e", 1234.5678);
questions.explanation: %e writes one digit before the point, 6 digits after it (the default precision, rounded) and an exponent of at least two digits: 1234.5678 = 1.2345678 x 10^3, printed as 1.234568e+03.
'A' + 2 is 67, the code of C. %c prints C, %d prints the code 67, and c + 32 = 99 printed with %c is the lowercase letter c, because ASCII lowercase letters are 32 above the uppercase ones.

options: AB on the first line and C on the second line
A on the first line and BC on the second line
A, B and C on three separate lines
questions.explanation: printf writes exactly its text, while puts writes its string followed by a newline. So A and B share the first line, the newline comes after B, and C starts the second line.
%s skips leading whitespace and then stops at the first whitespace character, so only Ram is stored and Bahadur stays in the input buffer. A whole line needs fgets or a %[^\n] scanset.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%%d = %d", 5);
questions.explanation: %% is the conversion that prints one percent sign, so %%d prints the two characters %d. The following %d is a real conversion and prints the argument 5.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%+d|% d|% d]", 25, 25, -25);
questions.explanation: The + flag always prints a sign (+25). The space flag puts a blank where the plus sign would go for a non-negative value ( 25), while a negative value simply shows its minus sign (-25).

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%#o %#x %#X", 16, 31, 31);
questions.explanation: The # flag adds the base prefix: a leading 0 for octal (16 is 20 in octal, printed 020) and 0x or 0X for hexadecimal (31 is 1f). %X makes both the digits and the X uppercase.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%.4d|%6.3d]", 42, 7);
questions.explanation: For integer conversions the precision is the minimum number of digits, filled with leading zeros: %.4d gives 0042. In %6.3d the value first becomes 007 and is then right-justified with spaces in a field of 6.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%*.*f]", 9, 3, 3.14159);
questions.explanation: Each * takes its value from the argument list, so the width is 9 and the precision 3. 3.14159 rounded to 3 decimals is 3.142 (5 characters), right-justified in 9 columns with 4 leading spaces.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%.2s|%5.3s]", "Nepal", "Nepal");
questions.explanation: For %s the precision is the maximum number of characters printed: %.2s gives Ne. %5.3s takes the first 3 characters, Nep, and right-justifies them in a width of 5 by adding 2 spaces.
Converting -1 to a 32-bit unsigned int gives 2^32 - 1 = 4294967295, with all 32 bits set. %u prints it in decimal and %x prints the 8 hexadecimal digits ffffffff.
printf returns the number of characters it wrote. The opening bracket, the 5-column field '   42' and the closing bracket make 1 + 5 + 1 = 7 characters, so n = 7.

questions.questionText:
What happens when the following statement is executed?
printf("%d", 10, 20);
options: It prints 10; the extra argument is evaluated but ignored
Compile error: too many arguments to printf
questions.explanation: The C standard says that when the format is used up, any remaining arguments are evaluated but otherwise ignored. A compiler may warn, but the program compiles and prints 10.

questions.questionText:
Assume the ASCII character set. What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%d", putchar('A') + 1);
questions.explanation: The argument putchar('A') + 1 is evaluated before printf runs: putchar prints A and returns the character written as an int, 65. Adding 1 gives 66, which printf then prints after the A.
getchar returns one character per call until the newline ends the loop. The 8 characters typed before Enter include 2 spaces, which are not counted, so n = 8 - 2 = 6.
The first %d stores 7. The blank skips the space, then the second %d meets x, which cannot start a number, so scanf stops, leaves b unchanged (2) and returns 1, the number of items stored.
The * in %*d suppresses assignment, so 20 is read and thrown away. x gets 10 and y gets 30, and scanf returns 2 because a suppressed conversion is not counted.
%d reads 5 and stops at the space. %c does not skip whitespace, so a receives that space. The blank before the second %c skips any whitespace (here none), so b gets x and y is left unread.
sprintf formats into buf instead of the screen and returns the number of characters stored, not counting the terminating '\0'. The string 12+30=42 has 8 characters, so n = 8.
fgets keeps the newline when it fits in the buffer, so s holds exam followed by '\n' and '\0'. strlen counts the 4 letters plus the newline, giving 5.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%-06d|%06.2d|%+06d]", 42, 42, 42);
questions.explanation: With the - flag the 0 flag is ignored, so %-06d left-justifies with spaces. For integer conversions a precision also cancels the 0 flag, so %06.2d pads 42 with spaces. %+06d prints the sign first and fills zeros after it: +00042.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%g|%g|%g", 0.00012, 123456.0, 1234567.0);
questions.explanation: %g keeps 6 significant digits and uses e-style only when the decimal exponent X is below -4 or at least 6. 0.00012 (X = -4) and 123456 (X = 5) are printed in fixed style with trailing zeros removed; 1234567 has X = 6, so it becomes 1.23457e+06.

questions.questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%d", printf("%d", printf("ABC")));
questions.explanation: The innermost printf runs first, printing ABC and returning 3. The middle printf prints 3 and returns 1 (it wrote one character). The outer printf prints that 1, so the screen shows ABC31.

A field width in scanf limits how many characters a conversion may read: %2d takes 12 and %3d takes 345. The last %d has no width, so it reads the remaining digits 67 and stops at the space, leaving 89 in the buffer.
%i reads an integer the way a C constant is written: a leading 0 means octal (010 = 8) and 0x means hexadecimal (0x1A = 26). %d always reads decimal, so the third 010 is stored as 10.

The scanset %9[^,] reads up to 9 non-comma characters, giving pen, and each literal comma in the format matches a comma in the string. qty = 12 and price = 7.5, so sscanf returns 3 and 12 x 7.5 = 90.00 is printed.

snprintf never writes more than sizeof s = 6 bytes, so s receives 5 characters, NEC-2, plus '\0'. It returns the length the complete text would have had, NEC-2024 = 8 characters, which lets the caller detect truncation.

fgets(a, 5, stdin) stores at most 5 - 1 = 4 characters, Kath, and leaves the rest of the line in the buffer. The second call continues from there and stores the next 4, mand; the u and the newline are still unread.

questions.questionText: Why is the & operator needed in scanf("%d", &n)?
options: & converts the typed characters into an integer
& tells scanf to skip leading whitespace
& is needed only when n has not been initialised
scanf needs the address of n so that it can store the converted value in n
questions.explanation: C passes arguments by value, so without & scanf would receive only a copy of n's value. Passing &n gives scanf the location of n, through which it writes the number it read.

questions.questionText: Which input function was removed from the C11 standard because it cannot limit the number of characters it stores and so can overflow the array?
questions.explanation: gets(s) keeps storing characters until a newline no matter how large s is, which causes buffer overflows. It was deprecated in C99 and removed in C11; fgets(s, n, stdin) is the bounded replacement.

questions.questionText: Which printf conversion specifier is intended for printing the value of a pointer (an address)?
questions.explanation: %p prints a void * value in an implementation-defined form, usually hexadecimal. Passing a pointer to %x or %u is a type mismatch (undefined behaviour) that visibly breaks where pointers are wider than int, and %a is for hexadecimal floating-point numbers.

questions.questionText: Which format specifier prints an unsigned int in hexadecimal using the uppercase letters A to F?
questions.explanation: %x and %X both print unsigned hexadecimal: %x uses a-f and %X uses A-F, so 255 prints as ff and FF respectively. %o prints octal, and there is no %H conversion.

questions.questionText: How does sprintf() differ from printf()?
options: sprintf writes the formatted text to the standard error stream
sprintf writes the formatted text into a character array instead of to stdout
sprintf ignores format specifiers and copies the text as it is
sprintf automatically adds a newline after the text
questions.explanation: sprintf(buf, format, ...) follows the same format rules as printf but stores the result, with a terminating '\0', in buf and returns the number of characters stored. Output to stderr is done with fprintf(stderr, ...).

questions.questionText: Which of the following output functions automatically writes a newline after the string it prints?
questions.explanation: puts(s) writes s followed by '\n'. fputs(s, stdout) and printf("%s", s) write exactly the string, and putchar writes a single character.

questions.questionText: Which call is equivalent to getchar()?
questions.explanation: getchar() is defined to behave like getc(stdin): it reads the next character from the standard input stream and returns it as an int, or EOF when no input is left.

questions.questionText: Given float f; double d; which statement about reading and printing these variables is correct?
options: Both scanf and printf accept %f for f and d alike, because float is promoted to double in both
printf needs %lf for d; printing d with %f shows only its float part
scanf needs %f for f and %lf for d, but printf("%f", ...) prints either one correctly
scanf needs %lf for f and %f for d
questions.explanation: A float passed to printf is promoted to double, so printf's %f always receives a double (%lf is accepted as a synonym). scanf receives pointers, which are not promoted, so it must be told whether it is storing a float (%f) or a double (%lf).

questions.questionText: Why should the value returned by getchar() be stored in an int variable rather than a char?
options: getchar must be able to return EOF as well as every possible character value, and a char cannot represent all of these distinct results
Characters always occupy 4 bytes in C, so a char is too small for any character
putchar cannot print a value stored in a char variable
Assigning the result of getchar to a char is a compile error in C
questions.explanation: getchar returns an unsigned char value converted to int (0 to 255 with 8-bit chars) or EOF, which is negative. Stored in a char, EOF is either never matched (unsigned char) or confused with the byte 0xFF (signed char), which breaks loops such as while ((c = getchar()) != EOF).

questions.questionText:
char line[80];
What does scanf("%79[^\n]", line); do?
options: It reads one word, stopping at the first space or newline
It reads the whole line and stores the newline at the end of line
It skips every character up to the newline and stores nothing
It reads up to 79 characters, including spaces, and stops before the newline, which stays in the input buffer
questions.explanation: [^\n] is a scanset that accepts every character except a newline, so spaces are stored too, and 79 limits the count so line cannot overflow. Unlike fgets, this conversion does not consume the newline; it remains in the buffer.

questions.questionText: A program shows progress with printf("Working...") (no newline) and reports errors with fprintf(stderr, ...). Why can an error message appear on a terminal before "Working..." does?
options: stdout is buffered, so text without a newline can wait in the buffer, while stderr is not buffered and is written at once
stderr has a higher priority, so the operating system interrupts stdout to print it
printf output without \n is discarded and never appears
fprintf is faster because it does not parse its format string
questions.explanation: On a terminal stdout is line-buffered, so "Working..." stays in the buffer until a newline, fflush(stdout) or normal program exit. stderr is never fully buffered (in practice it is unbuffered), so an error message is written immediately and can overtake it.

questions.questionText:
long long big = 9000000000LL;
In printf("%lld", big), what does the ll in the conversion specification indicate?
options: That the value is left-justified in its field
That the value is printed with a minimum width of two columns
That the corresponding argument has type long long int
That the value is printed in scientific (long) notation
questions.explanation: ll is a length modifier: it tells printf, and likewise scanf, that the argument is a long long int (unsigned long long with %llu). Other length modifiers are h for short, l for long and L for long double (%Lf); left-justification is the - flag and width is a plain number.

questions.questionText: Which statement about field width and precision in printf is correct?
options: A width smaller than the number of digits truncates the number to that many digits
A width smaller than the output never truncates it, but a precision on %s can cut a string short
In %.3d the precision keeps only the last 3 digits of the number
A field width has no effect on %s conversions
questions.explanation: The width is only a minimum, so printf("%2d", 12345) still prints 12345. For %s the precision is a maximum, so %.3s prints at most 3 characters, while for %d it is a minimum digit count filled with zeros.

questions.questionText: Which statement about EOF is correct?
options: EOF is the character '\0' stored at the end of every file
EOF is defined as 0 so that loops such as while (c) stop at the end of input
EOF is a negative int constant defined in stdio.h, returned by input functions at end of input or on a read error
EOF is a special byte written to disk after the last character of every text file
questions.explanation: EOF is a macro for a negative integer (commonly -1) that getchar, getc, scanf and similar functions return when no more input is available or an error occurs. It is not a character stored in the file; '\0' is the string terminator.

questions.questionText: Which statement about scanf format strings is NOT correct?
options: A literal character in the format, such as the / in "%d/%d", may be missing from the input without affecting the later conversions
A whitespace character in the format matches any amount of whitespace in the input, including none
%c does not skip leading whitespace, unlike %d, %f and %s
%*d reads an integer but neither stores it nor counts it in the return value
questions.explanation: Ordinary characters in the format must match the input exactly; if the / is missing, scanf stops there, the remaining conversions are not performed and the return value shows how many succeeded. The other three statements are standard scanf rules.

subtopics.title: Control Statements & Looping
subtopics.subtitle: if/else ladders, switch rules, the three loops, break/continue/goto and loop-count traps

concepts.text: Selection: if, if-else, Ladders and Nesting
Forms of the if statement:
items: Simple if: the statement (or block) runs only when the condition is non-zero; if (x) is the same as if (x != 0).
if-else: exactly one of the two branches runs.
Nested if: an if inside another; the dangling-else rule pairs an else with the NEAREST unmatched if, regardless of indentation.
else-if ladder: conditions are tested top to bottom, the first true branch runs and the rest are skipped; the final else is optional.
Braces are optional for a single statement, but a semicolon straight after if (...) makes an empty body, so the next statement always runs.
The conditional operator cond ? a : b is an expression form of if/else and can be used inside other expressions.

concepts.text: switch-case
Rules of switch:
items: The controlling expression must be of an integral type: int, char, short, long or enum. float, double, strings and arrays are not allowed.
Each case label must be a compile-time integer constant (case 1:, case 'a':, case MAX: with #define); no variables, no ranges like 1..5 and no duplicate labels.
Execution jumps to the matching case and then continues into the following cases until a break or the end of the switch: this is fall-through.
default is optional, may appear anywhere (usually last) and runs when no case matches; without default an unmatched value does nothing.
break leaves the switch; a continue inside a switch refers to the enclosing loop, not the switch.
Several labels may share one body (case 'a': case 'e': ...), which is intentional fall-through.
switch tests only equality against constants; an else-if ladder is needed for ranges and floating-point tests. switch is usually clearer and faster (jump table) for menus.

concepts.text: The Three Loops

rows: Menus and input validation that must run once

concepts.text:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)        /* init; test; update */
    printf("%d ", i);              /* 0 1 2 3 4 */

int n = 0;
while (n < 3) { n++; }             /* body runs 3 times, n = 3 */

int m = 10;
do { m++; } while (m < 5);         /* runs ONCE although 10 < 5 is false: m = 11 */

for (;;) { break; }                /* all three parts are optional: infinite loop */
for (i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--) ;   /* comma operator in init and update */
for-loop mechanics:
items: The initialisation runs once; the condition is tested before every iteration (a false condition at the start means zero iterations); the update runs after the body, then the test repeats.
When the loop ends normally the counter holds the first value that failed the test: after for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) the value of i is 5.
C99 allows a declaration in the init part; that variable exists only inside the loop.
for (;;) and while (1) are the idiomatic infinite loops; a missing update (while (i < 10) with no i++) is an accidental one.
Nested loops: the inner loop runs to completion for every iteration of the outer one, so bodies execute n x m times.
Avoid float counters: for (f = 0; f != 1.0; f += 0.1) may never stop because 0.1 is not exact in binary.

concepts.text: Jump Statements: break, continue, goto
Transferring control:
items: break leaves the innermost enclosing loop or switch immediately, and only that level: a break in an inner loop does not stop the outer loop.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the update part of a for loop or to the condition of a while / do-while loop.
goto label; jumps unconditionally within the same function; its accepted use is escaping from deeply nested loops in one step.
return leaves the whole function from any depth of nesting; exit() from stdlib.h ends the program.
break and continue are legal only inside loops (break also inside switch); elsewhere they are compile errors.

concepts.text: Counting Iterations and Classic Bugs
How many times does the body run?
items: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times (i = 0..n-1); for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) also runs n times (i = 1..n) but with different values of i.
for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) runs n + 1 times: the classic off-by-one.
for (i = n; i > 0; i--) runs n times; for (i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) runs 4 times (0, 3, 6, 9).
for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) runs ceil(log2 n) times: n = 100 gives 7 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64).
while (n) { n /= 10; count++; } counts the digits of n; while (n > 0) with n = 0 runs zero times but do { } while (n > 0) runs once.
Nested for i < n and j < n gives n^2 body executions; i < n and j < i gives 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) = n(n - 1)/2.

concepts.text: Bugs that MCQs are built around:
items: if (x = 5) assigns 5 and is always true; if (x = 0) is always false. The comparison is ==.
for (i = 0; i < 5; i++); with a stray semicolon has an empty body; the block that follows runs once with i = 5.
while (i < 10); with a semicolon is an infinite loop, as is any loop whose condition variable is never updated.
for (unsigned i = 5; i >= 0; i--) never ends because an unsigned value is always >= 0 (it wraps to 4294967295).
A missing break in a switch silently runs the following cases; a break inside an inner loop does not exit the outer loop.
A variable declared in the for header (C99) does not exist after the loop; using it there is a compile error.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Tracing Loops, switch Internals and Jumps

Every for loop can be rewritten as a while loop: for (init; cond; update) body behaves like init; while (cond) { body update; }. The only difference is continue, which still runs the update in the for form but would skip it in the while form. To predict output, trace the loop in a table with one column per variable plus the condition, add a row for every test, and stop at the first row whose condition is false. The values in that row are the values the program sees after the loop.

rows: for (i = a; i <= b; i += s), a <= b

concepts.plainText: for (i = n; i > 0; i /= 2) runs floor(log2 n) + 1 times (n = 50 gives 6)

concepts.text:
Output:
1
10
101
1010

Trace (the inner loop runs j = 1..i and prints j % 2):
i = 1: j = 1          -> 1
i = 2: j = 1, 2       -> 1 0
i = 3: j = 1, 2, 3    -> 1 0 1
i = 4: j = 1, 2, 3, 4 -> 1 0 1 0
Inner iterations: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 = 4 x 5 / 2
switch details beyond the basic rules:
items: The integer promotions are applied to the controlling expression, so a char or short is compared as an int; labels may be constant expressions such as 'a' + 1 or 2 * 3.
Two labels that evaluate to the same value, such as case 4: and case 2 * 2:, are a compile error even though they are written differently.
Labels may be written in any order and default may sit anywhere; if default is not last and has no break, control falls into the case written after it.
Statements placed after the opening brace but before the first case label are never executed.
A break inside a switch leaves only the switch; a continue inside a switch that is inside a loop continues that loop.
Compilers often turn a dense set of case values into a jump table, which is why a switch can be faster than a long else-if ladder.

concepts.text:
Output:
2 2

Trace:
i = 0: s[0] = 'l' -> default, c = 1; s[1] = 'o' is not '\0', repeat
i = 1: s[1] = 'o' -> vowel,   v = 1; s[2] = 'o', repeat
i = 2: s[2] = 'o' -> vowel,   v = 2; s[3] = 'p', repeat
i = 3: s[3] = 'p' -> default, c = 2; s[4] = '\0', stop
The five stacked labels share one body, and break stops the fall into default.
More loop traps worth tracing carefully:
items: while (n--) tests the old value, so it runs n times and leaves n at -1; while (--n) tests the new value, runs n - 1 times (for n >= 1) and leaves n at 0.
A comma inside a condition, as in i < 3, j < 5, evaluates both tests but uses only the last one (j < 5).
In a while or do-while loop, a continue placed before the update skips that update, so the loop may never end; in a for loop the update still runs.
while (i++ < 3) increments i even on the failing test: starting from 0, the body runs 3 times and i ends at 4.
Changing the counter inside the body adds to the header's step: for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) { i++; } advances by 2 per pass and runs 5 times.
goto can jump backward to build a loop, but only within one function; it can never jump into another function.

rows: The first statement after that loop or switch
Innermost enclosing loop (never a switch on its own)
The update of a for loop, or the test of a while or do-while
Any nesting depth within the same function
The labelled statement, forward or backward
The caller, together with the returned value

concepts.text: For loop-output questions, list the counter values until the first one that fails the test, and remember that side effects in that failing test (such as n--) still happen. For switch questions, mark the entry label first, then read straight down until a break or the closing brace, ignoring the other labels on the way.

formulas.plainText: for (i = a; i < b; i += s) runs ceil((b - a)/s) times; i <= b runs floor((b - a)/s) + 1 times
for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) runs ceil(log2 n) times (n = 100 gives 7)
nested i < n, j < n gives n^2 iterations; i < n, j < i gives n(n - 1)/2
max = (a > b) ? a : b;

notes.text: if (x = 5) assigns and is always true. The comparison is x == 5. Writing the constant first, if (5 == x), turns the slip into a compile error.

do-while always executes at least once, even when the condition is false from the start, because the test comes after the body. MCQs often pair this with a while loop that runs zero times on the same data.
A semicolon right after for (...) or while (...) is a legal empty statement: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++); printf("%d", i); prints 3 exactly once, and while (x < 5); with no body loops forever.
break exits only the innermost loop or switch. To leave two nested loops at once use a flag variable, a return, or a goto to a label after the outer loop.

formulas.title: Iterations of a counted for loop
formulas.plainText: for (i = a; i < b; i += s) runs ceil((b - a)/s) times
formulas.description: With <= the count is floor((b - a)/s) + 1; for step 1 this is b - a versus b - a + 1, the source of every off-by-one question.

formulas.title: Doubling loop
formulas.plainText: for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) runs ceil(log2 n) times
formulas.description: A counter that doubles (or halves) each time runs a logarithmic number of times: n = 100 gives 7 iterations, n = 1024 gives 10.

formulas.title: Nested loop counts
formulas.plainText: independent nested loops: n * m; triangular (j < i): n(n - 1)/2
formulas.description: The inner body runs once for every combination of outer and inner values; a triangular inner bound gives the sum 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1).

formulas.title: for loop syntax
formulas.plainText: for (init; condition; update) { body }
formulas.description: init runs once, condition is checked BEFORE each iteration, update runs after the body; all three parts are optional and for (;;) loops forever.

flashcards.front: Difference between while and do-while?
flashcards.back: while checks the condition before the body (may run zero times); do-while checks after, so the body always runs at least once and the statement ends with a semicolon.

flashcards.front: Which types may a switch expression have, and what may a case label be?
flashcards.back: Only integral types (int, char, short, long, enum), never float, double or strings; each case label must be a distinct compile-time integer constant.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between break and continue?
flashcards.back: break leaves the innermost loop or switch immediately; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and goes to the loop's update/condition.

flashcards.front: How many times does for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) run, and what is i afterwards?
flashcards.back: n + 1 times (i = 0 to n); afterwards i equals n + 1, the first value that failed the test.

questions.questionText: Which statement skips the remaining statements of the current loop iteration and goes on with the next iteration?
questions.explanation: continue abandons only the rest of the current pass; the loop then goes on with its update (for) or its test (while and do-while). break leaves the loop entirely and return leaves the whole function.

questions.questionText: In the loop for (initialisation; condition; update) statement, which part is executed exactly once?
questions.explanation: The initialisation runs once, before the first test. The condition is evaluated before every iteration (and once more when it fails), the update after every iteration, and the body once per iteration.

questions.questionText: In a switch statement that has no default label, what happens when the value of the expression matches none of the case labels?
options: The whole switch body is skipped and execution continues after the switch
questions.explanation: default is optional. Without it, a value that matches no case label makes nothing inside the switch run; control passes to the statement after the closing brace.

questions.questionText: Which loops of C are entry-controlled, i.e. test their condition before executing the body?
questions.explanation: while and for evaluate the condition before each iteration, so their body may run zero times. do-while is exit-controlled: it tests after the body, so its body always runs at least once.

questions.questionText: Which of the following ends the whole program immediately, even when it is executed inside a function called from main?
questions.explanation: exit(), declared in stdlib.h, terminates the program from any function after flushing the output streams. return leaves only the current function, and break and continue affect only the innermost loop or switch.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a syntactically correct do-while loop in C (i is an int)?
questions.explanation: A do-while loop has the form do statement while (expression); and, unlike while and for, it must end with a semicolon after the closing parenthesis. The condition always comes after the body.

questions.questionText:
int x = 1;
Which statement, written directly inside main and not inside any loop or switch, causes a compile error?
options: if (x) goto end;   (with a label end: later in main)
questions.explanation: break is allowed only inside a loop or a switch; an if statement is neither, so the compiler rejects it. goto to a label in the same function and return are legal anywhere in main.

questions.questionText: When a continue statement is executed inside a for loop, where does control go next?
options: Directly to the condition test, skipping the update
To the update expression, and then to the condition test
To the first statement after the loop
questions.explanation: In a for loop continue jumps to the end of the body, so the update (such as i++) still runs before the condition is tested. In while and do-while loops it goes straight to the condition, which is why a continue placed before a manual update can cause an infinite loop.

questions.questionText: In nested if statements written without braces, how does the compiler decide which if an else belongs to?
options: It pairs the else with the outermost if
It uses the indentation of the else
It pairs the else with the nearest preceding if that does not already have an else
It reports an ambiguity error and refuses to compile
questions.explanation: This is the dangling-else rule: an else always binds to the closest unmatched if in the same block. Indentation is ignored, so braces are needed to attach an else to an outer if.

questions.questionText:
int x = 10;
Which case label, used inside switch (x), causes a compile error in C?
questions.explanation: A case label must be an integer constant expression. Character constants, arithmetic on constants and macros that expand to integers all qualify, but a string literal is an array, not an integer constant.

questions.questionText: Which statement about goto in C is correct?
options: It can jump to a label in any function of the program
It can only jump forward, never backward
The target label must be declared before it is used, like a variable
It can transfer control only to a label in the same function
questions.explanation: Labels have function scope, so goto may jump forward or backward within the function but never into another function. A label is just an identifier followed by a colon and needs no declaration; it may appear after the goto that uses it.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the switch statement is NOT correct?
options: The default label must be the last label in the switch
The controlling expression may have type char
Two case labels in the same switch cannot have the same value
When a matching case has no break, execution falls through into the next case
questions.explanation: default may appear anywhere inside the switch; putting it last is only a convention, and if it is not last and has no break, control falls through into the case written after it. The other three statements are standard rules.

questions.questionText: Which of the following tests cannot be written directly as a C switch statement and needs an if-else ladder instead?
options: Choosing an action for menu options 1 to 4 stored in an int
Counting vowels by examining a char variable
Checking whether a double temperature t lies between 20.5 and 30.0
Handling each value of an enum type
questions.explanation: switch compares a value of integer type for equality with constant labels. It cannot test ranges or floating-point values, so a condition such as t >= 20.5 && t <= 30.0 needs if-else.

questions.questionText: A loop is written as for (i = 0; ; i++). What does the missing condition mean?
options: It is treated as always false, so the body never runs
It is treated as always true, so the loop runs until a break, return or goto leaves it
It is a compile error; only the initialisation and update may be omitted
The loop body runs exactly once, like a do-while
questions.explanation: Any of the three parts of a for header may be left out. An omitted condition is replaced by a non-zero constant, so for (;;) and for (i = 0; ; i++) are infinite loops unless a jump statement ends them.

subtopics.title: User-Defined & Recursive Functions
subtopics.subtitle: Prototypes, definitions, call by value, scope and storage, recursion with worked examples

concepts.text: Why Functions and Their Three Parts

A function is a self-contained block of code that performs one task and can be called from anywhere in the program. Functions give modularity, reuse, easier testing and shorter programs. Library functions such as printf and sqrt come with the compiler; user-defined functions are written by the programmer. Every user-defined function involves three things: a declaration (prototype) that tells the compiler the name, return type and parameter types; a definition that contains the body; and one or more calls. If the definition appears after main, the prototype is mandatory in C99 because implicit int declarations were removed.
Anatomy of a function:
items: Return type: any type except an array; void means nothing is returned (a bare return; is optional). main returns int.
Parameter list: type and name for each parameter; void f(void) takes none. In C, f() means 'unspecified parameters' (C89 style), so write void explicitly.
Formal parameters appear in the definition; actual arguments appear in the call. Arguments are matched by position and converted to the parameter types.
return expr; sends back exactly one value, converted to the return type, and ends the function; a function may contain several return statements.
Functions cannot be defined inside other functions in C (no nesting), but any function may call any other, including itself.
A call to a function with no prototype in sight is an error in C99 and a warning in older compilers; prototypes for library functions live in the headers.

concepts.text: Call by Value and Call by Reference
Parameter passing in C:
items: Call by value is the only mechanism in C: the function receives a COPY of each argument, so changing a parameter never changes the caller's variable.
Call by reference is simulated by passing an address with & and receiving it in a pointer parameter; the function then modifies the original through *p.
Arrays are the apparent exception: an array name decays to the address of its first element, so a function can modify the caller's elements.
To return more than one value, pass pointers to the result variables or return a struct.
C++ adds true references (void f(int &r)), function overloading and default arguments; those belong to the C++ subtopics.

concepts.text: Scope, Lifetime and Storage Classes
Scope and storage rules inside functions:
items: Local (auto) variables and parameters exist only inside their function or block; they are created fresh on every call and destroyed on return, so their values are not retained.
Two functions may use the same local names without conflict; a local with the same name as a global shadows (hides) the global inside that block.
Global variables are declared outside all functions, are visible from the declaration to the end of the file, are zero-initialised and are shared by every function that uses them.
static local: initialised once (default 0), stored in the data segment and keeps its value between calls: the idiom for call counters.
extern declares a global defined in another file; register asks for a CPU register and forbids &; auto is the default for locals and is never written in practice.
In short: storage class decides where a variable lives (stack, register, data segment), how long it lives (block or whole run) and its default value (garbage or 0).

concepts.text: Recursion

Recursion is a function calling itself, directly or through another function. A correct recursive function has a base case that returns without a further call and a recursive case that moves the problem closer to the base case. Every call gets its own stack frame with its own parameters and locals; the frames pile up until the base case is reached and then unwind, each returning its result to its caller. Without a reachable base case the stack grows until the program crashes (stack overflow). Any recursion can be rewritten as iteration, but recursion is the natural fit for factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, power, Towers of Hanoi, binary search and tree traversal.

long fact(int n) {                        /* n! = n * (n-1)!, 0! = 1 */
    if (n <= 1) return 1;                 /* base case */
    return n * fact(n - 1);               /* fact(4) = 4*3*2*1 = 24 */
}
int fib(int n) {                          /* 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13 ... */
    if (n < 2) return n;                  /* fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1 */
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);       /* two calls: O(2^n) time */
}
int gcd(int a, int b) {                   /* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) */
    return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b);    /* gcd(48,18)->(18,12)->(12,6)->(6,0) = 6 */
}
int power(int x, int n) { return n == 0 ? 1 : x * power(x, n - 1); }  /* x^n */

Loop repeats inside one stack frame
One frame per active call: O(depth)

concepts.text: Counting calls is a common question: fact(n) makes n calls (depth n) and runs in O(n); the naive fib(n) makes about 2^n calls because each call spawns two, which is why fib(40) is visibly slow while a loop is instant. Finally, a function pointer stores the address of a function: int (*fp)(int, int) = add; then fp(2, 3) calls add, which is how callbacks such as the comparator of qsort work.
Going Deeper: Recursion, Call Counts and Function Pointers

A function call is a fixed sequence: the caller evaluates the arguments, the values are copied into the parameters of a new stack frame together with the return address, and control jumps to the function. When return runs, its value is handed back and the frame is discarded. In recursion every active call has its own frame, so the name n refers to a different variable in each call. Two numbers describe a recursion and must not be confused: the depth is the largest number of frames alive at one moment (it decides stack use), while the total number of calls is how many frames are ever created (it decides running time).

The Tower of Hanoi shows how a recurrence gives a closed form. To move n disks from A to C, move the top n - 1 disks to the spare peg B, move the largest disk to C, then move the n - 1 disks from B onto it. The move count therefore obeys T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1, giving 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ... Adding 1 to both sides gives T(n) + 1 = 2(T(n - 1) + 1), so T(n) + 1 doubles at every step and equals 2^n. The smallest disk moves on every other move, 2^(n - 1) times in all.

concepts.plainText: T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1, so T(n) = 2^n - 1 (3 disks: 7 moves, 5 disks: 31, 10 disks: 1023)

concepts.text: Function pointers, lifetimes and common mistakes:
items: int (*fp)(int, int) = add; declares fp as a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning int; without the parentheses, int *fp(int, int); declares a function that returns int *.
A function name decays to its address, so fp = add and fp = &add are equivalent, and fp(2, 3) and (*fp)(2, 3) both call add.
An array of function pointers such as int (*op[3])(int, int) = {add, sub, mul}; replaces a switch with a table lookup: op[choice](a, b).
Passing a function pointer as a parameter creates a callback: qsort calls the programmer's int cmp(const void *, const void *) for every comparison.
Never return the address of an automatic local: its frame is gone after the return. Return the value, or the address of a static or malloc'ed object.
In C a static local must be initialised with a constant expression (static int n = 0; is fine, static int n = f(); is not), and the initialisation happens only once.
Changing a parameter never changes the caller's argument, and in recursion n-- inside one call does not alter n in the caller's frame; f(n--) even passes the old value and recurses forever.

concepts.text: To trace a recursive function, write one line per call with its argument, then unwind from the deepest call upward. Statements before the recursive call run in call order (on the way down); statements after it run in reverse order (on the way back). Count calls with a recurrence such as C(n) = 2C(n - 1) + 1 rather than by listing every call.

notes.text: Every recursive function needs a reachable base case; without one the call stack overflows. fact(-1) with if (n == 0) as the only base case never stops because n goes -1, -2, ... (use n <= 1).

Call by value means swap(x, y) with plain int parameters leaves x and y unchanged; the answer to 'what is x after the call' is its original value. Only a version taking int * (called with &x, &y) swaps them.

Calling a function defined below main without a prototype is an error in C99 (implicit declaration). Prototypes end with a semicolon; definitions do not, and a semicolon after the definition's closing brace is harmless but a semicolon after the header line is an error.
A static local keeps its value between calls but is still invisible outside the function; a global keeps its value and is visible everywhere. Both are zero-initialised, unlike an ordinary local.

formulas.title: Factorial recursion
formulas.description: The textbook recursive definition: fact(4) = 4 * fact(3) = 24, and a recursive fact(n) makes n calls with stack depth n.

formulas.title: Fibonacci recursion
formulas.description: Two base cases and two recursive calls per step give the sequence 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13; the naive version costs about 2^n calls.

formulas.title: Euclid's GCD
formulas.plainText: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b); gcd(a, 0) = a

flashcards.front: What is recursion? What must every recursive function have?
flashcards.back: A function calling itself. It must have a base case that stops the recursion (or the stack overflows) and a recursive case that moves toward the base case.

flashcards.front: Prototype vs definition of a function?
flashcards.back: A prototype (int add(int, int);) declares the name, return type and parameter types and ends with a semicolon; the definition supplies the body in braces and is written exactly once.

flashcards.front: How can a C function change a variable belonging to the caller?
flashcards.back: Only by receiving its address: pass &x and declare the parameter as a pointer (int *p), then write through *p. Plain parameters are copies (call by value).

flashcards.front: What does show(3) print if show prints n before the recursive call show(n-1) and again after it (base case n == 0)?
flashcards.back: 3 2 1 1 2 3: the first prints happen on the way down, the second set while the calls unwind in reverse order.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a valid C prototype for a function avg that takes two int arguments and returns a double?
questions.explanation: A prototype is return type, name and a parenthesised list of parameter types, ended by a semicolon; names are optional. 'int a, b' leaves b without a type, the third declares the wrong types, and the return type must come first.

questions.questionText: In a C function prototype, the names of the parameters are:
options: Optional; only the types are required, and any names given need not match the definition
Mandatory, and they must match the names used in the definition
Mandatory, but they may differ from the names used in the definition
Not allowed; a prototype may list only the types
questions.explanation: The compiler checks calls against the number and types of parameters, so int add(int, int); and int add(int x, int y); are equivalent prototypes. Names in a prototype are only documentation and may differ from the definition.

questions.questionText: In the call area(len, 5), what are len and 5 called?
questions.explanation: The values written in a call are the actual arguments; the names in the function header that receive copies of them are the formal parameters.

questions.questionText: In C11, how does the declaration int f(); differ from int f(void); ?
options: They are identical: both declare a function that takes no arguments
int f(); declares a function taking one int argument by default
int f(void); is a syntax error in C; void is allowed only as a return type
int f(); says nothing about the parameters, so calls are not checked, while int f(void); declares that f takes no arguments
questions.explanation: In C (up to C17) an empty list is an old-style declaration with unspecified parameters, so f(1, 2) still compiles; with (void) the compiler rejects any argument. Only C++ (and C23) treat f() as taking no parameters.
The prototype says sq takes exactly one int, so a call with two arguments violates the prototype and is rejected. 3.5 is simply converted to int, and ignoring a return value (sq(4);) is legal.

questions.questionText: A C function must change the value of the caller's int variable x. How should it be called and declared?

Call f(*x) and declare the parameter as int *p
Call f(&x), declare the parameter as int *p and assign through *p
Call f(x) and declare the parameter as int &p
questions.explanation: C only passes copies, so the function needs the address of x: f(&x) with an int * parameter, and *p = value writes into x itself. int &p is a C++ reference and is not valid C.
Through p the function changes a: *p = 2 + 3 = 5. q is a copy of b, so q = 3 + 5 = 8 is returned into c while b stays 3, giving 5 3 8.

questions.questionText: How many values can a C function send back to its caller with one return statement?

None; results must be passed through global variables
Exactly one value, although that value may be a whole struct

questions.explanation: Objects with static storage duration (globals and static locals) are zero-initialised before the program starts; only automatic locals start with indeterminate values.

questions.questionText: How does a static local variable differ from a global variable?
options: The static local is destroyed when its function returns
The static local lives on the stack, the global in the data segment
The static local starts with a garbage value, the global with 0
The static local is visible only inside its function, although both keep their values for the whole run
questions.explanation: Both have static storage duration: one copy, zero-initialised, alive for the whole program. The difference is scope: a static local can be named only inside its own block, a global from its declaration to the end of the file.

questions.questionText: Where are the automatic (local) variables and parameters of a C function normally stored, and when do they cease to exist?
options: On the stack, in the function's frame; they disappear when the function returns
In the data segment; they disappear when the program ends
On the heap; they disappear when free() is called
In the code segment next to the function; they never disappear
questions.explanation: Each call pushes a stack frame holding its parameters and auto locals, and the frame is popped on return. That is why their values are not kept between calls and why their addresses must not be used after the return.

questions.questionText: Which storage class, applied to a variable declared outside all functions, gives it internal linkage so that other source files cannot access it?
questions.explanation: static at file scope limits the name to its own translation unit (internal linkage). extern declares a name defined elsewhere, and auto and register apply only to block-scope variables.

questions.questionText: C functions are classified as library functions and user-defined functions. Which of the following is a user-defined function?
questions.explanation: The programmer writes the body of main() in every program (the system only calls it), so it is classed as a user-defined function. printf() and scanf() come ready-made from <stdio.h> and sqrt() from <math.h>, so they are library functions.
Each call adds the last digit n % 10 and recurses on n / 10: 6 + 9 + 0 + 4 + sd(0) = 19.

questions.questionText: What is the minimum number of moves needed to solve the Tower of Hanoi with 5 disks?
questions.explanation: T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1 gives T(n) = 2^n - 1, so T(5) = 32 - 1 = 31 moves.

questions.questionText: In the standard recursive Tower of Hanoi solution for 6 disks, how many times is the smallest disk moved?

questions.explanation: Direct recursion is a function calling itself; when the cycle passes through another function it is indirect or mutual recursion. A prototype is needed so that the first function can call the second before its definition.

questions.questionText: Which statement about recursion and iteration is correct?
options: Recursion always uses less memory than the equivalent loop
A recursive function runs faster than a loop because it needs no condition tests
Every recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively, if necessary with an explicit stack
Problems such as the Tower of Hanoi cannot be solved without recursion
questions.explanation: Recursion and iteration are equally powerful: a loop plus an explicit stack can imitate any recursion. Recursion usually costs more time (call overhead) and memory (one frame per active call).

questions.questionText: When a function calls itself, what does each active call get?
options: Its own stack frame holding its own copies of the parameters and automatic local variables
One shared set of local variables used by all the active calls
Its own copy of every global variable
Its own copy of the function's machine code
questions.explanation: Every call pushes a new frame with fresh parameters, auto locals and a return address, so n in one call is a different variable from n in the call below it. Globals, statics and the code are shared.

questions.questionText: A recursive call is called a tail call when:
options: It is the first statement in the function
It is the last action of the function, so nothing is left to do after it returns
questions.explanation: In return gcd(b, a % b); the call's result is returned unchanged, so it is a tail call; in return n * fact(n - 1); a multiplication is still pending. Compilers can turn tail calls into jumps, removing the stack growth.

questions.questionText: Which statement about where functions may be defined in standard C is correct?
options: A function may be defined inside the body of another function, where it becomes local to that function
Every function must be defined outside all other functions; functions may call one another, but their definitions cannot be nested
Only main may contain the definitions of other functions
A function may be defined inside another function only if it is declared static
questions.explanation: Standard C allows function definitions only at file scope, so one definition can never be placed inside another, although any function may call any other function that has been declared. GCC accepts nested functions only as a non-standard extension, and Clang rejects them.

questions.questionText: In the call qsort(arr, n, sizeof(int), cmp); from <stdlib.h>, what is cmp?
options: The number of comparisons qsort may perform
A macro from stdlib.h that selects ascending order
An array of flags giving the sort order of each element
A pointer to a comparison function written by the programmer, which qsort calls back
questions.explanation: qsort receives the address of a function int cmp(const void *, const void *) and calls it whenever it must compare two elements. Passing a function pointer in this way is a callback.

Nothing: x keeps its value because its address was returned

subtopics.title: Arrays & String Manipulation
subtopics.subtitle: 1-D, 2-D and multi-dimensional arrays, row-major addresses, C-strings and <string.h>

concepts.text: One-Dimensional Arrays

An array is a fixed-size collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory and accessed by an index that runs from 0 to size - 1. The declaration type name[size]; needs a constant size in C89 (C99 also allows variable-length arrays). Local arrays without an initialiser contain garbage; = {0} sets every element to zero, a partial initialiser zero-fills the remaining elements, and int a[] = {1, 2, 3} infers the size from the list. C does no bounds checking: reading or writing a[5] in a 5-element array compiles and silently corrupts memory.

int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};    /* a[0] = 10 ... a[4] = 50 */
int b[5] = {1, 2};                  /* rest are 0: 1 2 0 0 0 */
int c[] = {7, 8, 9};                /* size inferred: 3 */
int n = sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]);   /* 20 / 4 = 5 elements */
a[5] = 99;                          /* out of bounds: NO check, undefined */
printf("%d %d\n", a[2], *(a + 2));  /* 30 30 */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(c));         /* 12 */
printf("%d\n", a == &a[0]);         /* 1 */
Array facts:
items: Elements are contiguous, so &a[i] = base address + i * sizeof(type); for int a[5] at address 1000, &a[3] is 1012.
The array name is a constant pointer to the first element: a == &a[0] and a[i] == *(a + i), but a = b and a++ are errors.
sizeof(a) is the whole array in bytes (n * sizeof(type)) inside the scope where it is declared; sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) gives the element count.
Arrays cannot be assigned or compared with = and ==; copy with a loop or memcpy and compare element by element.
Static and global arrays are zero-initialised; local arrays are not.

concepts.text: Two-Dimensional and Multi-Dimensional Arrays

int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};   /* 2 rows, 3 columns */
int k[2][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4};             /* row-major fill: {1,2,3},{4,0,0} */
int r[][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};        /* only the FIRST size may be omitted */
printf("%d\n", m[1][2]);                /* 6 */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(m));             /* 2 * 3 * 4 = 24 bytes */
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++)
        printf("%d ", m[i][j]);         /* 1 2 3 4 5 6 */
int cube[2][3][4];                      /* 3-D: 2*3*4 = 24 ints, cube[i][j][k] */
Row-major storage and addressing:
items: C stores a 2-D array row after row: m[0][0], m[0][1], m[0][2], m[1][0], ... so the last index varies fastest.
Address of m[i][j] = base + (i * cols + j) * sizeof(type); for int m[3][4] at 2000, &m[2][1] = 2000 + (2 * 4 + 1) * 4 = 2036.
m[i] is the i-th row, itself an array of cols elements, and decays to a pointer to m[i][0]; m[i][j] == *(*(m + i) + j).
A 3-D array a[d1][d2][d3] holds d1 * d2 * d3 elements and &a[i][j][k] = base + ((i * d2 + j) * d3 + k) * sizeof(type).
When a 2-D array is a parameter every dimension except the first must be given: void f(int a[][3], int rows).
Matrix addition, transpose and multiplication (an r1 x c1 times a c1 x c2 matrix gives r1 x c2) are the standard 2-D array programs.

concepts.text: Arrays and Functions

When an array is passed to a function its name decays to a pointer to the first element, so the function receives an address rather than a copy: changes made through the parameter are visible to the caller, which makes array passing behave like call by reference. Because only the address arrives, sizeof(arr) inside the function is the pointer size (4 or 8), and the element count must be passed as a separate argument. int arr[] and int *arr are interchangeable as parameter declarations. A function cannot return an array by value; it returns a pointer to a static or dynamically allocated array instead.
C-Strings

char s[] = "HELLO";        /* 6 bytes: H E L L O \0 */
char t[10] = "HI";         /* H I \0 then 7 unused bytes */
char u[] = {'H', 'I', '\0'};   /* same as "HI" */
char *p = "HELLO";         /* pointer to a string literal: read-only */
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(s), strlen(s));   /* 6 5 */
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(t), strlen(t));   /* 10 2 */
s[0] = 'J';   printf("%s\n", s);             /* JELLO */
printf("%s\n", s + 1);                       /* ELLO */
printf("%c\n", s[strlen(s) - 1]);            /* O: last character */

concepts.text: String facts and pitfalls:
items: A string is a char array terminated by the null character '\0' (ASCII 0); "A" is a 2-byte string while 'A' is a single char.
A string can be initialised at declaration but not assigned later: s = "HI"; is an error, use strcpy(s, "HI").
== on two strings compares addresses, not contents; use strcmp(a, b) == 0 for equality.
sizeof counts the '\0' (and any unused bytes of a bigger array), strlen stops at the first '\0': printf("%s", "Hello\0World") prints Hello.
scanf("%s") stops at whitespace and has no bound; use %29s or fgets. Modifying a string literal through char *p = "HI" is undefined behaviour.
ctype.h gives toupper, tolower, isalpha, isdigit; stdlib.h gives atoi, atof, strtol to convert strings to numbers.
An array of strings is char names[3][20] (fixed rows) or char *names[] = {"a", "bb"} (pointers to literals).

char b[20] = "xy", a[] = "abc";
strcat(b, a);   printf("%s\n", b);                 /* xyabc */
printf("%d\n", strcmp("abc", "abd") < 0);          /* 1: negative result */
printf("%d\n", strcmp("B", "a") < 0);              /* 1: 'B' (66) < 'a' (97) */
printf("%s\n", strchr("hello", 'l'));               /* llo */
printf("%s\n", strstr("license", "cen"));           /* cense */
char x[] = "hi", y[] = "hi";
printf("%d %d\n", x == y, strcmp(x, y) == 0);       /* 0 1: == compares addresses */
char w[4]; strcpy(w, "exam");                       /* OVERFLOW: needs 5 bytes */
Going Deeper: Array Addressing and String Internals

The row-major formula follows from counting. For an array with M rows and N columns, reaching m[i][j] means skipping i complete rows of N elements each and then j more elements in row i, so the element sits i × N + j places after the first one; multiplying by the element size w gives the byte offset. Column-major order, used by Fortran and MATLAB, stores whole columns one after another, so the count becomes j × M + i. Languages whose indices may start at another lower bound, such as Pascal's A[1..10], subtract the bounds first, while C indices always start at 0. Because the compiler needs N to evaluate the formula, every dimension except the first must appear in a parameter declaration.

concepts.plainText: Row-major: Loc(A[i][j]) = B + w * ((i - Lr) * N + (j - Lc)), where N = number of columns and Lr, Lc = lower bounds (0 in C)
Column-major: Loc(A[i][j]) = B + w * ((j - Lc) * M + (i - Lr)), where M = number of rows

concepts.text: Details of the <string.h> functions that questions like to test:
items: strncpy(d, s, n) copies at most n characters; if s is shorter it pads d with '\0' up to n, and if s has n or more characters it writes no terminator at all.
strcat(d, s) starts writing at the '\0' of d, so d must already hold a terminated string and have room for strlen(d) + strlen(s) + 1 bytes.
strcmp compares characters as unsigned char values and stops at the first difference or at the end; the standard guarantees only the sign of the result, not a value such as 1 or -1.
strchr(s, c) and strrchr(s, c) return a pointer into s (subtract s to get the index) or NULL; the terminating '\0' counts as part of the string, so strchr(s, '\0') points at the end.
strstr(s, t) returns a pointer to the first occurrence of t or NULL, and an empty t matches at once, so strstr(s, "") returns s.
strlen walks the whole string on every call, so for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++) can cost O(n²) steps; store the length in a variable first.
fgets keeps the newline the user typed, while scanf("%s") stops at the first space or newline and leaves the rest in the input buffer.

concepts.text: Before an address calculation, settle four things: row-major or column-major order, the lower bounds (always 0 in C), the element size in bytes, and whether the given base is the address of the first element. The answer is then base + (number of elements skipped) × (element size).

questions.questionText: Which of the following declarations is INVALID in C?

questions.questionText: A global array int g[4]; is declared outside all functions without an initialiser. What are its elements at program start?
options: g[0] is 0 and the rest are garbage

questions.questionText: Given the declarations int a[3] = {1, 2, 3}, b[3]; which statement is correct?

a == b compares the two arrays element by element

Copying in place overwrites values before they are read: a[0] = a[4] = 5, a[1] = a[3] = 4, a[2] = 3, then a[3] = a[1] (now 4) and a[4] = a[0] (now 5). A real reversal swaps pairs up to the middle.

The array automatically grows to 11 elements
An array-index-out-of-bounds exception is raised at run time
Nothing checks the index: the write goes outside the array and the behaviour is undefined

questions.questionText: The array double m[5][6] is stored in C's row-major order starting at address 1200, and a double occupies 8 bytes. What is the address of m[3][4]?
questions.explanation: Address = base + (i * cols + j) * size = 1200 + (3 * 6 + 4) * 8 = 1200 + 176 = 1376. Column-major order would give 1200 + (4 * 5 + 3) * 8 = 1384.

questions.questionText: A two-dimensional array A[1..10][1..15] (rows 1 to 10, columns 1 to 15) of 2-byte elements is stored row by row, and A[1][1] is at address 500. What is the address of A[6][8]?
questions.explanation: Subtract the lower bounds first: 500 + ((6 - 1) * 15 + (8 - 1)) * 2 = 500 + 82 * 2 = 664. Column-major order would give 500 + (7 * 10 + 5) * 2 = 650, and ignoring the lower bounds gives 696.

questions.questionText: The array int x[4][5] starts at address 1000 and an int occupies 4 bytes. Which element is stored at address 1068?
questions.explanation: The offset is (1068 - 1000) / 4 = 17 elements. In row-major order 17 = i * 5 + j gives i = 3 and j = 2; x[1][4] would be the column-major reading (17 = 4 * 4 + 1).

questions.questionText: The array int c[2][3][4] starts at address 4000 and an int occupies 4 bytes. What is the address of c[1][2][3]?
questions.explanation: Offset = ((i * d2 + j) * d3 + k) * size = ((1 * 3 + 2) * 4 + 3) * 4 = 23 * 4 = 92 bytes, so the address is 4000 + 92 = 4092.

questions.questionText: In C, which statement about the declaration char a[3] = "ABC"; is correct?
options: It is a compile error in C, because the string needs 4 bytes
The compiler silently enlarges a to 4 elements
a holds 'A', 'B' and '\0'; the 'C' is dropped

options: Both a[0] = 'H' and p[0] = 'H' are allowed

questions.questionText: Which <string.h> function appends a copy of one string to the end of another?
questions.explanation: strcat(d, s) writes s starting at the terminating '\0' of d. strcpy overwrites d from the start, strcmp compares and strstr searches for a substring.

questions.questionText: Assuming the ASCII character set, which of the following does the C standard guarantee about the value returned by strcmp("cat", "car")?
